newsitem.title: USA: NY utilities consider options after court ruling.
newsitem.headline: NY utilities consider options after court ruling.

text.p: New York's electric utilities are considering their options, including appeal, after a court ruling that state regulators have the authority to implement electric industry competition, New York State Energy Association President Howard Shapiro said Tuesday.
The court ruled Tuesday the legislature has properly delegated the commission with the necessary authority to carry out its Competitive Opportunities Opinion.
"The Public Service Law is a blueprint within which the Public Service is charged with the govcernance of the energy resources of the State of New York," the ruling said.
"We're dissapointed," Shapiro said, noting this is the first level of judicial appeal.
The association is giving "serious consideration to our various options, including appeal," he said.
Shapiro also pointed out Judge Joseph Harris of the State Supreme Court, Albany County, ruled that the utilities' suit was premature on some points.
Specifically, the ruling pointed out, "the courts have held that judicial review is not appropriate when 'the effect on the plaintiff...is incomplete and undetermined'."

The suit was filed in September by the association and its eight utility members -- Brooklyn Union Gas Co, Long Island Lighting Co, Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Orange & Rockland Utilities Inc, Central Hudson Gas and Electric Corp, Niagara Mohawk Power Corp, Rochester Gas & Electric Corp and New York State Electric & Gas Corp.
The ruling said the motion to annul the Public Service Commission's call for restructuring of the electric industry "is in all respects denied."

Besides the commission's jurisdiction, the court said, the petition raised three other issues -- did the commission's rejection of the utilities' demand that all competitive losses be born by consumers breach a regulatory compact, violate the Public Service Law or infringe on the utilities constitutional rights;
-- can a utility challenge a policy statement that does not order the actions contested; and
-- did the commission comply with the State Administrative Procedure Law.
On the matter of cost recovery, "irrespective of the impact that such rates would have on consumers or a state's economy," the ruling said "the courts have answered no."
